t: Subject to the availability of appropriations, section 102301(d) of title 54, United States Code, is amended by striking “not more than $7,000,000” and inserting “not more than $9,000,000”.

fable.w: This section only raises a dollar cap in section 102301(d) of title 54 from $7,000,000 to $9,000,000, subject to appropriations. There is no tempting participation reading: it involves no consultation, hearing, comment period, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue, and no party outside the federal government takes part in any federal decision.

opus.w: This section only raises a funding cap in an existing statute from $7,000,000 to $9,000,000. It does not create a comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, or right to sue. The mere fact that it amends another provision does not bring any participation process into this section.
opus.s: is amended by striking “not more than $7,000,000” and inserting “not more than $9,000,000”
opus.b: I'd label this **No**. A tempting reading is that the amended provision, section 102301(d) of title 54, might set up some program involving outside parties. But that program isn't described here. This section only changes a dollar cap.

qwen_chat.w: This section is a simple appropriation amendment that increases a funding cap. It does not establish any process for consultation, comment, or coordination with parties outside the federal government. There are no advisory boards, public hearings, or requirements for state/local input mentioned.
qwen_chat.s: Subject to the availability of appropriations, section 102301(d) of title 54, United States Code, is amended by striking “not more than $7,000,000” and inserting “not more than $9,000,000”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that changing a funding cap affects who can participate in a program, but the text itself contains no procedural mechanism for outside involvement. It is purely a budgetary amendment.
